name: Felix Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Felix, 27, and I lead a team of six on home and contents claims at the regional office of Hartwell Insurance, which is one of the big national firms. I live with my partner Lena, who's a nursery nurse, in a rented terrace near the old mill. We're both on modest pay, and between us we've got maybe three weeks of bills in the bank after the car died in the summer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are burst pipes, storm damage and the odd kitchen fire, all coming in through the portal. I sort them by how bad they are, hand them out to the team, and take the big ones myself, the ones where a family is in a hotel. I use the firm's summary tool now and then for long email chains, which saves me ten minutes. The best part is when I get a surveyor out the same day; the worst part is the targets on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was good news for workers, and that we should keep an eye on how firms use even the small stuff. As the union rep I'd tell the team the summary tool is fine but the targets are the real problem. Online I wouldn't post much, I'm not that guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job would be fine, but our money wouldn't suddenly be fine. My partner Lena and I are one broken boiler away from the credit card, and that's true whatever AI does. Hartwell keeps shutting regional offices too, which was happening before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the team and keep using the summary tool where it helps. I'd push, through the union, for the targets to be looked at, since nobody can say AI is doing the work. And Lena and I would finally set up a savings pot, even if it's forty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, a bit tired. It's the same worry I already have, rent and the car and an office that might close. AI just isn't the thing keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Hartwell closing regional offices. How real is that for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They shut the office in Norbridge two years ago and moved the work to the city. Our building lease ends in 2028, and nobody will tell us if they're renewing. If they don't, it's an hour and a half each way, and we don't have a reliable car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena cut first if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the trip to see her parents at Christmas, because the train is expensive. Then eating out, which is already once a month. We've talked about it, and we'd both rather keep the cheap gym than the takeaways.

say: I'd call it **good news** for workers, while keeping an eye on small tools.
I'd tell the team as union rep that the **targets**, not the summary tool, are the problem.
think: My job is fine, but Lena and I are one **broken boiler** from the credit card.
Hartwell closing **regional offices** worries me more than AI, and that was happening already.
do: **Keep leading** the household claims team and using the summary tool for long emails.
**Raise the targets** through the union branch.
Open a joint **savings pot** with Lena at £40 a month.
feel: Mostly **steady** but **tired** from the same money worries.
S0.quote: My partner Lena and I are one broken boiler away from the credit card, and that's true whatever AI does.
fieldNote: His real threat is an **office closure**, with the lease ending in 2028.
He is a calm, practical **union rep**, more comfortable in meetings than online.
Household money is **thin on both sides**, since his partner is also low paid.

steps.text: Keep leading the household claims team as now
Raise the claims targets at the next union branch meeting
Open a joint savings pot with Lena at £40 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to be at the table before the software goes in, not after. I'd tell my team straight that some of our work will move to the system and we need a say in which bits. I'd probably write a calm post for the branch newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think our team goes from six to three within a few years. Sorting claims, checking cover and writing letters are exactly the thinking tasks you listed. I'm the lead, so I might be one of the three, but I wouldn't bet our rent on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Hartwell to put me on the pilot for the new claims system, because I'd rather learn it early than late. I'd push for a written agreement on redeployment, no compulsory cuts for two years. And Lena and I would stop the car loan idea and keep the old bus pass life a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. I'd be fine some days, then see the numbers in a team meeting and feel sick. Having a plan helps, but it doesn't fix the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who joined last year and is brilliant on the phone but slow on the system. And Dev, who's fifty and has a mortgage. If it's three out of six, I'd be fighting for the people who'd struggle most to find another job here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to be on the pilot, but you're also fighting the cuts. Do those sit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they do, because if I don't understand the system I can't argue about it. You can't negotiate about a claims system you've never used. I'd rather be the rep who knows exactly what it can and can't do.

say: I'd say the union needs a **seat at the table** before the software goes in.
I'd tell my team plainly that some of our work will **move to the system**.
think: I expect the team to drop **from six to three** within a few years.
Being team lead might save me, but I **wouldn't bet** our rent on it.
do: **Volunteer** for the pilot of the new claims system.
**Push for a deal** with no compulsory cuts for two years.
**Drop the car loan** idea and keep using the bus.
feel: **Worried** some days and fine on others, depending on the **numbers** he sees.
S1.quote: You can't negotiate about a claims system you've never used.
fieldNote: He sees learning the system as a **bargaining tool**, not a betrayal.
He names specific colleagues he would **protect**, which shows his rep instincts.
He accepts that his own job could **realistically go**, so anxious fits despite his calm tone.

steps.text: Volunteer for Hartwell's pilot of the new claims system
Push for a two-year no-compulsory-cuts agreement
Drop the car loan and keep commuting by bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the government to step in, with income support and a real plan, not speeches. I'd organise a branch meeting the first week. Online I'd probably share more than usual, because people would need to see others are angry too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think home claims are done within a year or two of 2028. Home claims are nearly all reading, checking and deciding, so I'd be in the first wave. The surveyors who go out to houses might get until 2031, but I don't have their skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the surveyor I work with most, Tomasz, about whether I could train as a loss adjuster's assistant, the person who visits the damage. I'd sit down with Lena and work out how long her wage covers the rent alone, which is maybe two months. And I'd be in every union meeting about redundancy terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I'm normally the steady one in the room, and I don't think I could be. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're not going to lose the house, even if I wasn't sure. Then later I'd admit I didn't know. She'd say her nursery isn't going anywhere for a while, which would be true and a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the surveyors get until 2031. Is that hands-on work a real option for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Hartwell paid for the training, which I doubt they would in a panic. It's a few years of climbing into lofts and looking at damp. I'd do it, but I'd be starting at the bottom on even less money.

say: I'd call for **income support** and a real government plan, not speeches.
I'd organise a **branch meeting** in the first week and share more online.
think: Home claims are nearly all **thinking work**, so I'd be in the **first wave**.
Surveyors visiting houses might last **until 2031**, but I don't have their skills.
do: **Ask Tomasz** (a surveyor) about training as a loss adjuster's assistant.
Work out with Lena how long **her wage** alone covers the rent.
**Attend every union meeting** on redundancy terms.
feel: **Frightened**, losing his usual role as the **steady one**.
S2.quote: Home claims are nearly all reading, checking and deciding, so I'd be in the first wave.
fieldNote: He clearly sees the **three-year gap** for hands-on work and looks toward surveying.
Lena's nursery job is the household's **anchor**, which shapes his relief.
He expects to **lose his job** within two years and can't sleep, so alarmed fits.

steps.text: Ask Tomasz about training as a loss adjuster's assistant
Work out with Lena how long her wage covers rent
Attend every union meeting on redundancy terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's long enough to plan if we start now. I'd want the union pushing Hartwell for a retraining fund straight away. I'd tell friends to stop pretending it's science fiction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still lose the job, just in 2031 instead of 2028. Five years is a chance to move toward the hands-on side, the surveying, because that buys roughly three more years after that. I'd be 32, and I'd hate starting again, but I'd be young enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask Hartwell to let me shadow Tomasz on site visits one day a fortnight. I'd look into the loss adjusting certificate, which I think takes about eighteen months part-time. Lena and I would aim for three months' savings by cutting the Christmas trips for a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but busy, which is better than worried and stuck. I'd still lose sleep over 2031. Seeing AGI five years out is like seeing a storm on the forecast a week out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money for the certificate come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the problem, it's about a thousand pounds. I'd push the union to get Hartwell to pay, since they'd be saving on my wage soon. If not, I'd pay in instalments and we'd skip a holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd say to the younger people on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Priya to get out of desk claims while she's young, honestly. She's good with people, and that counts for something on a site visit. I'd tell her quietly, though, not in a team meeting.

say: I'd say five years is short but **long enough** to plan if we start now.
I'd want the union to push Hartwell for a **retraining fund** straight away.
think: I'd still **lose the desk job**, just in 2031 instead of 2028.
Moving to **surveying** could buy me roughly three more years after AGI.

Start the **loss adjusting certificate**, about 18 months part-time.
**Skip Christmas trips** to build three months' savings.
feel: **Worried but busy**, like seeing a **storm** forecast a week out.
S3.quote: Seeing AGI five years out is like seeing a storm on the forecast a week out.
fieldNote: The extra time lets him **plan a route** into hands-on work, but the loss is still expected.
The **£1,000 course fee** is a real barrier on his money.
He'd quietly advise juniors to **leave desk claims**, unlike his public union line.

steps.text: Shadow Tomasz on site visits one day a fortnight
Take the loss adjusting certificate part-time over 18 months
Skip Christmas trips to build three months' savings
Push the union branch for a Hartwell retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for anyone to be blindsided. I'd want the government to set up proper retraining with pay now, not in 2035. At work I'd say let's be the office that handled this well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable in a way the others don't. I'd be 37, and I could be a qualified loss adjuster by then, maybe even somewhere with a few more years left. My desk job still shrinks along the way, though, and our money is still thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hartwell and keep leading the team while it lasts. I'd do the loss adjusting certificate over two or three years, paced so we can afford it. I'd also start using the AI tools properly, because by 2030 nobody will hire an adjuster who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. It feels like there's a path. I'd still be watching the lease on our office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier that the targets were the real problem. Does that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if anything they'd get worse while the software comes in, because they'll measure us against it. I'd still be fighting the targets in year three. That bit of the job never goes away until the job does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Lena change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids in a few years. With ten years' warning, my partner Lena and I would still have kids, but we'd wait until I'd finished the certificate. With two years' warning, I honestly don't think we would.

say: I'd say a decade means **no excuse** for anyone to be blindsided.
I'd ask the government for **paid retraining** now, not in 2035.
think: At **37** I could be a qualified loss adjuster before AGI arrives.
My **desk job** still shrinks along the way, and our money stays thin.
do: **Keep leading** the team at Hartwell while the job lasts.
**Pace the certificate** over two or three years so it's affordable.
feel: **Calmer** but not calm, with a **path** in sight.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, my partner Lena and I would still have kids, but we'd wait until I'd finished the certificate.
fieldNote: The decade changes his **family plans** least, which shows how much time matters to him.
He would use AI tools to stay **employable** as an adjuster.
Income could still shrink, so he stays **anxious** rather than uneasy.

steps.text: Keep leading the Hartwell claims team
Do the loss adjusting certificate over two to three years
Learn the AI claims tools properly before 2030
Wait on children until the certificate is done

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to move to anything hands-on and our savings wouldn't last two months. What would help is paid retraining, a wage while you learn, and firms forced to tell staff early. A union contract that says so would help more than any speech.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people we help. When a family's kitchen burns down, they want a person on the phone. I'd want a rule that customers can always ask for a human, which would keep some of us in work too.

headlineQuote: When a family's kitchen burns down, they want a person on the phone.
portrait: Felix is a 27-year-old **team lead** on home claims at a big insurer's regional office.
He lives with Lena, a nursery nurse, with **three weeks** of bills saved.
As a steady **union rep**, he learns new systems so he can bargain about them.
He expects to lose his desk job under every AGI picture and eyes **loss adjusting**.
Ten years' warning lets him **plan kids** and a certificate; two years would not.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to move into hands-on work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a wage, early notice, and a right to a **human** for customers.
